title: The Sisters of the Levee
premise: Three blocks west of the mansions, two sisters from Virginia operate the most notorious establishment in Chicago, appointed with gold cuspidors and a $15,000 piano. Prairie Avenue affects ignorance of the route.

opening.text:
JAUNT: THE SISTERS OF THE LEVEE. Dusk on a Monday in November 1904, at Eighteenth Street and Prairie Avenue.

Four stops, proceeding west from Millionaire's Row toward the Levee, the city's red-light district, and concluding at a church on its periphery. Prairie Avenue lies three blocks from the most celebrated address in Chicago, and it is not the Glessner House. Two sisters who adopted the surname Everleigh opened a club on Dearborn Street in 1900, and some of the wealthiest men in the world have discovered its entrance.

Begin at the intersection, and observe which direction the cabs turn.

stops.text: Eighteenth and Prairie, as the gas lamps are illuminated. Eighteenth Street operates as a boundary: northward and eastward stand the mansions; southward and westward, "several blocks away from Prairie Avenue", commences the Levee, the district extending from Eighteenth Street to Twenty-second and from Wabash to Clark, which accommodates the city's most infamous brothels. The ladies of Prairie Avenue never acknowledge its existence. Nevertheless one of the two preeminent establishments in Chicago, Vic Shaw's, operated temporarily on Prairie Avenue itself. The two gentlemen hastening around this corner are not returning home. Follow them westward.

stage.caption: Two gentlemen in evening attire round the corner and proceed briskly west along Eighteenth Street.

cast.name: A gentleman out for the evening (unnamed)

stops.text: Indiana Avenue, one block west. Continue three blocks farther to Dearborn Street, where at 2131 and 2133 operates the Everleigh Club. Its proprietors are two sisters, Ada and Minna, who claim a Kentucky upbringing, which was "another story concocted by the sisters". They were born Simms, in Virginia, in 1864 and 1866. Utilizing an inheritance of approximately $35,000, they managed an establishment in Omaha before relocating to Chicago and purchasing an existing business on Dearborn. They derived their new surname from their grandmother, who concluded her correspondence "Everly yours". The club opened on 1 February 1900, deliberately refusing numerous callers that first evening. The Everleighs comprehended that in their enterprise, exclusivity established the price.

stage.caption: A gentleman descends the steps of an Indiana Avenue residence, consults his pocket watch, and turns west toward the Levee.

cast.name: A gentleman going out for the evening (unnamed)

stops.text: Farther south along Indiana, with the Levee two blocks west. The Everleigh Club comprises fifty rooms across two adjoining mansions: a Japanese Throne Room, a Mirror Room, a Silver Parlor, "a $15,000 gold-leafed piano for the Music Room" and "$650 gold cuspidors". Champagne costs $12 a bottle, "in an era when an entire meal could be had for fifty cents", and admission alone requires $50. Ada administers the accounts and recruits the women; Minna receives the clientele. In March 1902 Prince Henry of Prussia visited, and when a dancer's slipper dislodged and spilled champagne, a member of his entourage drank from it, initiating an enduring fashion. The establishment employs fifteen to twenty-five cooks and maids, and its women are designated "butterflies".

stage.caption: Two maids, released from duty, emerge from the side passage onto Indiana Avenue and hurry northward, conversing animatedly.

stops.text: First Presbyterian Church, at Indiana and Twenty-first Street, positioned at the Levee's eastern perimeter, near enough to hear it on summer evenings. According to persistent accounts, the club's distinguished clientele includes the actor John Barrymore and the authors Ring Lardner and Theodore Dreiser, and gossips append young Marshall Field Jr., who resides several blocks away. Subsequently "a rival madam maliciously accused the Everleigh sisters" of considerably worse, and that rumor proved ineradicable. The minister's entrance is illuminated, as is the club's. Tonight, as every night, the Levee is the more frequented of the two, a juxtaposition that exposes the distance between the city's professed morality and its actual conduct.

stage.caption: A family emerges from the church hall into the dusk as a cab passes in the opposite direction.

legs.story: West along Eighteenth Street, past the last of the mansions, to Indiana Avenue.
South along Indiana Avenue, with the Levee's commotion two blocks westward.
South to Twenty-first Street and the church at the Levee's perimeter.

endings.text: The walk concludes here. The Everleigh Club endured eleven years. On 24 October 1911 Mayor Carter Harrison Jr. ordered its closure, and Minna accepted the decision with characteristic composure: "If the Mayor says we must close, that settles it...I'll close up shop and walk out with a smile on my face". The building was demolished in July 1933. Prairie Avenue never conceded that it knew the route to Dearborn Street; it acknowledged only the route back, a selective memory that respectable society cultivated with remarkable consistency.

keepsake.title: A Card from the Levee
keepsake.text: An interpretive card concerning Chicago's Levee and the Everleigh Club around 1904; a reconstruction prepared for this walk, not a historical artifact.

evidence.text: Chicago's Levee District ran from Eighteenth Street to the north to Twenty-second Street to the south, Wabash to the east and Clark to the west, 'several blocks away from Prairie Avenue'.

The Everleigh Club and Vic Shaw's 'resort' were the preeminent brothels in Chicago, 'with Shaw's business existing on Prairie Avenue for a time.' Shaw lived until 1952 in a crumbling mansion at 2906 Prairie Avenue with a dog, cat and parrot.
evidence.locator: The post's second and last paragraphs.

evidence.text: The Levee's eastern edge, Wabash Avenue, lay three blocks west of Prairie Avenue, with Indiana and Michigan Avenues between.
evidence.reasoning: The blog gives the Levee's bounds as Eighteenth to Twenty-second, Wabash to Clark, 'several blocks away from Prairie Avenue'; the avenues between, Indiana and Michigan, are the city's grid west of Prairie.

evidence.text: The Sisters of the Levee: the day, Monday 21 November 1904, the hour and the order of the walk are this jaunt's framing, chosen because the stories meet on it (three days after Arthur Caton's death, a Monday of the Reading Class, before Kimball's death in December). No visit on that day is asserted.

The Sisters of the Levee: who is seen at each stop, where they stand, what they do and when are reconstructed. People with cards in the town play themselves; people the town has no card for (and the unnamed servants, callers and passers-by) are unnamed figures in period dress, and no likeness is claimed. No word anyone says is asserted.

The sisters were born Simms (in Greene County, Virginia, Ada in 1864 and Minna in 1866; the Kentucky childhood was 'another story concocted by the sisters'). With an inheritance of some $35,000 they ran a house in Omaha, then bought Effie Hankins's brothel at 2131-2133 South Dearborn, and took the name Everleigh from their grandmother, who signed her letters 'Everly yours'. The club opened on February 1, 1900, and turned away many of its first callers.

evidence.text: The club occupied two mansions, 50 rooms with themes such as the Japanese Throne Room, the Mirror Room and the Silver Parlor; it had 'a $15,000 gold-leafed piano for the Music Room' and '$650 gold cuspidors'. A bottle of champagne cost $12 'in an era when an entire meal could be had for fifty cents', and the entrance fee alone was $50.
evidence.locator: Other Ladies: the club paragraph; Wikipedia: History.

evidence.text: Ada, the quieter sister, kept the books and hired the women; Minna met the guests. The club employed '15 to 25 cooks and maids', and its women were called 'butterflies'.

evidence.text: On March 3, 1902, Prince Henry of Prussia visited the club; when a slipper came off during a dance and spilled champagne and one of his party drank from it, the custom of drinking champagne from a woman's shoe began.
First Presbyterian Church stood at Indiana Avenue and Twenty-first Street in 1904, two blocks west of Prairie Avenue and at the Levee's eastern edge.
evidence.reasoning: The church's own structure record dates it 1870-1873 to after 1911 and the 1911 Sanborn sheet draws it at Indiana and Twenty-first; the Levee ran east to Wabash, one block beyond Indiana and Michigan.

evidence.text: The blog names actor John Barrymore, authors Ring Lardner and Theodore Dreiser, and Marshall Field, Jr. among the club's famed clients, and says rumours persisted for years that the young Field had been shot there; Wikipedia: 'A rival madam maliciously accused the Everleigh sisters of murdering Field.'
evidence.locator: Other Ladies: the clients paragraph; Wikipedia: Scandals.

evidence.text: Mayor Carter Harrison Jr. ordered the club closed on October 24, 1911. Minna: 'If the Mayor says we must close, that settles it...I'll close up shop and walk out with a smile on my face.' The building was razed in July 1933.
